It was the first video game released for the emergent neural card technology and without question the most popular. People who were born BSS, before smart sync, didn’t have the right hardware integrated into their bodies but most of their children did and all of their grandchildren did. It was the dawn of the next generation in gaming. And in a world where unemployment had reached sixty percent, It was also a way for the idle youth to make a living wage. The legacy of the game however will always be the part it played in the fundamental shift in the direction of modern warfare.

The game was called goldfish and within forty eight hours of it’s release there were over ten million players across the United States. In a month a billion players in the allied territories of Europe and the Japanese controlled Pacific. It’s broad distribution was attributed primarily to it’s simplicity. There were no rules and you didn’t have to be taught how to play. Players just installed the software directly from the net, switched it on, and instantly the user would find themselves emerged in the game. By connecting directly into the human nervous system, the game used the body’s own five senses to transport the player into the world of the game.

The game started the same for every player. The user would wake up laying in the cool grass of an empty feild perceiving the world of the game through their own eyes. That is the default point of view but players can choose to go into a third person mode. If they do, they’ll realize that the character they are playing is a cat. Just a typical black cat at first glance like the kind you'd find in any home. A lot of players will continue as the default cat even after they realize that just by thinking it they can change the color of the cat to anything they want. As gamers begin to play, they’ll be able to move around the very small map which repeats if you reach the world’s edge.

After a while, from above gold fish will start to appear. The fish are brightly illuminated in a pulsating gold glow. Floating through space, the fish are covered in symbols and numbers that make up their scales and each of them have a clock somewhere on their bodies winding down quickly to midnight. The goal of every player is simply to touch as many of the fish as you can. If the clock reaches midnight before you can touch it, the fish disappears but there are always more then enough to keep you from running out. At first there are a dozen fish. Then there are fifty. Soon after that hundreds of them are floating around. Play long enough and you’ll see tens of thousands all at once. And the rewards for catching the fish are amazing.

Catching a fish in the game makes you feel like you’re eating your favorite food. It warms your soul like you're getting a kiss from the person who you have the strongest feeling for. It even feels better than all of that combined. Catching a fish is love, serenity, peace, and exhilaration all rolled into one. Plus as an added bonus each time you catch a fish, your coin account gets a tiny deposit. It’s not much just a fraction of a single coin. The smaller fish for example will earn you a thousanth of a coin while a the bigger ones can earn you a hundredth.

Sometimes, if you play for a really long time, you’ll start seeing other cats playing as well. That’s good because late in a gaming session, giant goldfish blink into existence that look as big as whales but can’t be touched alone. A team of players is needed to capture them. And that’s where you can earn as much as a whole coin for each player!

When a player catches a huge fish, it’s an incredible experience. They don’t just feel their own reward, which alone is an enormous flood of emotions. They feel the rewards of the other players in their team as well. Some players have even reported experiencing glimpses into the lives of the other players. They have watched entire life spans lived out in their own minds in the span of seconds. When a group of a hundred players or more reach for one of the massive fish that float through the game, the experience reported has been compared to omnipotence. Every hurt, every pain, every pleasure, every win that had ever been experienced by each of the players is experienced by all of the players.

Back in the real world where players lounge on couches or in beds, their minds gone to the world of the game, players can be seen with tears sliding down their cheeks as they are overwhelmed by the ecstasy produced from their emotional rewards. The Game has changed everything about life for devoted players. They don’t eat except to survive, they don’t sleep except when falling to overwhelming exhaustion. They play.

In an Excerpt from "The Age of Goldfish" by Professor of Psychology Reva O’Brien of UC Berkeley, he writes, The game exploits human being's natural tendency to be attracted to activities that help them escape reality. In 2050 when popular game consoles launched virtual reality headsets that let players step inside their favorite games, players were overwhelmed by the stunning and high definition 3D gaming which allowed a level of immersion that blurred the line between virtual reality and actual reality. The longer the player allowed themselves to remain in the virtual world, the more distressing reemergence into reality became. During a study conducted by UCLA's department of psychology players were reported experiencing feelings of depression and having thoughts of suicide when exposed to sessions of gaming lasting no longer than twelve hours. This effect which was considered extreme at the time was experienced with a technology that merely simulated visual and auditory stimuli. Goldfish reaches far beyond that. With integration directly into the player’s body’s, the game is generating it’s own neural patterns that are indistinguishable by the human brain to that of real world stimulation. The effects are multiplied by the game to an incalculable level. Such technology would seem to pose a risk to humanity's continued existence.

A warrant canary is a colloquial term for a regularly published statement that a service provider has not received legal process (like a national security letter) that it would be prohibited from disclosing to the public.
